target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly beneficial because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: AI is not good for society overall because its widespread deployment harms workers and small businesses, weakens critical thinking, replicates racism, and creates serious privacy risks; these harms are not minor side effects but central to how AI is used at scale.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is simply harmful overall because of jobs, cognition, bias, and privacy concerns
objection: Those harms do not show AI is inherently bad for society; they show AI needs safeguards, since it can augment work, act as a tutor that supports reasoning, reduce bias with audits and human oversight, and protect privacy with anonymization and on-device processing.

target: AG1’s reliance on safeguards such as reskilling, tutoring design, auditing, anonymization, and on-device inference
objection: Those safeguards are structurally unlikely to be implemented well at scale, and even when they are, they do not remove the core harms; profit-driven deployment still causes displacement, cognitive shortcutting, biased outcomes, and privacy inference risks.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards are too unreliable or idealized to make AI net beneficial
objection: It is a false choice to treat governance as either perfect or useless; regulation, audits, transparency, phased rollouts, and liability can meaningfully reduce harms, while AI’s accessibility, health, and workplace-safety benefits remain concrete and significant.

target: AG1’s argument that regulation and accountability can make AI responsibly deployable
objection: AI harms are hard to measure and control because models are opaque, frequently updated, and owned by private firms that do not fully disclose their systems, so audits and transparency are incomplete and safeguards tend to be reactive and uneven while deployment keeps scaling.

target: AG2’s claim that opacity, frequent updates, and private ownership make AI governance fail in practice
objection: Those governance difficulties do not justify concluding AI is net harmful; continuous monitoring, post-deployment evaluation, red-teaming, standardized documentation, and privacy techniques like differential privacy or federated approaches can still manage risk and preserve AI’s social benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring, red-teaming, and privacy techniques can manage AI at scale
objection: Those safeguards may work in narrow pilots but do not solve the scaling problem: monitoring at scale can itself require more data collection and surveillance, while documentation and red-teaming cannot anticipate all emergent failures across many domains and updates.

target: AG2’s claim that scale makes AI harms dominate its benefits
objection: The scale problem applies to harms, but AI can also be part of the defense: it can detect scams, fraud, deepfakes, and abuse; privacy-preserving monitoring can avoid full surveillance; and enforceable high-level rules can reduce misuse without needing to predict every failure mode.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can mitigate AI-driven harms through automated detection, moderation, and watermarking
objection: AI-based defenses create new harms because automated moderation and detection can disproportionately suppress racial minorities, dissenters, and smaller creators, while watermarking and provenance systems are easy to bypass or strip and depend on uneven adoption across platforms.
